lessons.summary: Interrogate what a source can reveal by connecting content, origin, purpose and historical context.
objectives: Infer from source content.
Evaluate value and limitation in relation to a question.
Corroborate across sources.
keyIdeas: A source is valuable for some questions and limited for others.
Origin does not automatically determine reliability.
Corroboration compares both agreement and difference.

definitions.meaning: Information about a source’s origin, creator, time and context.
Comparison with other evidence to test or extend a claim.
The intended outcome or audience effect of a source.

method: Read content before provenance.
Make a specific inference and cite its evidence.
Connect origin or purpose to a precise value or limitation.
Compare with another source or missing perspective.

workedExample.prompt: Evaluate a mayor’s campaign speech as evidence about living conditions.
steps: Content may identify issues the campaign expects voters to recognise.
The public persuasive purpose can reveal political priorities.
The same purpose may encourage selective examples or exaggeration.
Resident records or independent data could corroborate the claims.
workedExample.conclusion: The speech can be valuable for political priorities and public messaging, but it cannot establish typical living conditions on its own.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing “biased, therefore useless”.
misconceptions.correction: Bias can itself provide evidence about viewpoint, priorities and intended audience.

misconceptions.mistake: Listing origin, purpose, value and limitation without linking them.
misconceptions.correction: Explain why each feature matters for the exact historical question.

practice.prompt: A factory poster warns workers to protect machinery during wartime. Infer one priority of its creator.
hints: Use a detail from the source description.
solution: The creator prioritises maintaining industrial production, shown by the instruction to protect machinery.

practice.prompt: Evaluate a soldier’s private letter as evidence of army morale.
hints: Consider immediacy, audience and representativeness.
solution: A private letter may reveal personal feelings close to the event.
The writer may still self-censor to reassure family or avoid military censorship.
One soldier cannot represent the whole army.

practice.prompt: Two newspapers report the same protest differently. Explain how you would use both accounts.
hints: Difference can be evidence.
solution: Compare reported events, language, images, ownership, audience and publication timing.
Agreements may establish common facts.
Differences may reveal selection or political perspective and should be tested against independent evidence.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching source: a shop notice lists early opening hours beside a message aimed at railway workers. Infer one intended audience need.
hints: Link opening time to the named audience.
Do not invent purchasing behaviour.
solution: The notice suggests the shop is appealing to workers needing access before their shifts or journeys.
The early hours and named railway audience support that inference, but do not prove how many workers shopped there.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: a museum catalogue omits domestic servants from a short list of notable residents. Does this prove no servants lived in the town?
hints: Consider selection and purpose.
Absence from one list is not a population census.
solution: A selective catalogue may omit people outside its chosen focus.
Household or employment records would be needed; the omission alone does not establish absence.

checklist: I connect provenance to the question.

notes.title: An advertisement supports a bounded claim
paragraphs: A source can be valuable even when its author has a clear interest in persuading an audience. The task is to identify what it can support for a particular inquiry. A recruitment advertisement may reveal the promises used to attract workers without proving that actual conditions matched those promises. Distinguish the words or features observed from the inference drawn from them. Corroboration works best when sources have sufficiently independent origins and address comparable events or conditions. Silence also needs caution: an omitted topic may reflect purpose, space or survival of records rather than the absence of the historical activity.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional teaching source: a workshop recruitment advertisement promises regular wages and a warm room. Assess its use for studying recruitment priorities.
steps: The promises show which benefits the advertiser chose to emphasise to prospective workers.
They do not independently establish that workers received those conditions.
workedExamples.conclusion: The advertisement is useful for public recruitment priorities; payroll and worker testimony would test fulfilment.

flashcards.front: Does bias make a source useless?
flashcards.back: No; its value depends on the inquiry.

flashcards.front: What is an observation about a source?
flashcards.back: A feature directly present in its content or form.
A reasoned conclusion drawn from observed evidence.
Repeated claims may derive from one original account.

diagrams.title: An advertisement supports a bounded claim
diagrams.description: Promised conditions reveal persuasion before they establish lived experience.

nodes.label: Recruitment promise
nodes.detail: Regular wages and a warm room

nodes.label: Supported inference
nodes.detail: These benefits were emphasised to attract workers

nodes.label: Unresolved outcome
nodes.detail: Actual wages and room conditions need separate evidence

lessons.summary: Build causal arguments by distinguishing triggers, conditions, motives and relative importance.
objectives: Construct causal chains.
Rank causes using explicit criteria.
Use evidence to handle interaction and contingency.
keyIdeas: Events usually have multiple interacting causes.
A trigger accelerates change but may depend on deeper conditions.
Importance must be judged against a criterion such as necessity, reach or timing.

definitions.meaning: An event that immediately accelerates or initiates a larger development.
A longer-term condition shaping what actions or outcomes are possible.
The role of uncertain circumstances and choices that were not inevitable.

method: Define the outcome and time frame.
Group causes by type or chronology.
Trace mechanisms with specific evidence.
Compare importance using one consistent criterion and address interaction.

workedExample.prompt: How should an essay treat a protest that begins after a sudden price increase?
steps: Identify the price increase as a possible trigger.
Investigate prior wages, food access, organisation and political trust as conditions.
Explain how the trigger activated those conditions.
Test whether protest would likely have occurred without each factor.
workedExample.conclusion: The answer should not confuse the last event before protest with the only or deepest cause.

misconceptions.mistake: Listing causes in separate paragraphs without comparison.
misconceptions.correction: Show interaction and compare each cause using the same criterion.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating chronological closeness as importance.
misconceptions.correction: A proximate trigger may be less necessary than a long-term enabling condition.

practice.prompt: Distinguish a trigger from a structural cause.
hints: Contrast immediate event and long-term condition.
solution: A trigger immediately accelerates an outcome.
A structural cause is a longer-term condition that makes the outcome more likely or shapes its form.

practice.prompt: Explain how an economic grievance and political organisation can interact to cause protest.
hints: Neither factor acts alone.
solution: Grievance creates motivation but may remain private.
Organisation provides communication, leadership and coordination.
Together they turn dissatisfaction into collective action.

practice.prompt: “Leadership was the most important cause of the movement’s success.” Develop a method for judging this claim.
hints: Define success and importance first.
solution: Define success through outcomes and time frame.
Compare leadership with resources, participation, opponents and context.
Test necessity, reach and counterfactual evidence.
Reach a qualified judgement that accounts for interaction.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: poor harvests raise food prices, while a neighbourhood network organises a petition. Explain how the two factors could interact.
hints: Separate grievance from collective action.
Link organisation to expressing the grievance.
solution: High prices create a shared grievance about food access.
The network coordinates signatures and action, converting that grievance into an organised petition.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: a festival begins after a new mayor takes office. No planning records are supplied. Evaluate “the mayor alone caused the festival”.
hints: Timing does not reveal who planned or funded it.
Look for alternative contributors.
solution: The timing is compatible with the claim but does not establish the mayor’s role.
Planning, funding and community records are needed to assess earlier plans and other contributors before attributing sole causation.

checklist: I define the outcome and period.

notes.title: Transport change can enable market expansion
paragraphs: Historical causes operate through mechanisms rather than merely appearing before an event. A transport improvement can lower journey costs, enabling traders to reach new markets, but the outcome also depends on demand and available goods. Long-term conditions, immediate triggers and enabling factors may interact. Calling one cause necessary means the outcome could not have occurred without it under the argument’s assumptions; calling it sufficient means it could produce the outcome without additional requirements. These are demanding claims. A careful explanation compares timing, mechanism and alternative influences, and recognises that counterfactual conclusions cannot be observed directly.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional case: a canal opens, freight charges fall and merchants begin selling in a distant town. Explain a plausible causal chain and a limit.
steps: The canal may reduce transport costs, making sales to the distant market financially feasible.
Merchant records linking route choice, costs and sales would strengthen the mechanism.
workedExamples.conclusion: The sequence supports a plausible explanation but does not exclude rising demand or other changes.

flashcards.back: The process through which one factor produces an outcome.
No; it is necessary for many claims but not sufficient evidence.
A condition that makes an outcome possible or easier.

flashcards.front: What does a necessary-cause claim assert?
flashcards.back: The outcome would not occur without that factor under the stated account.

diagrams.title: Transport change can enable market expansion
diagrams.description: Each link needs evidence, not chronology alone.

nodes.label: Canal opens
nodes.detail: A new freight route becomes available

lessons.summary: Evaluate a source for a particular historical question by connecting what it says with how and why it was produced.
objectives: Link provenance to a specific evidential use.
Distinguish stated purpose from inferred purpose.
Explain value and limitation without automatic reliability labels.
explanation: Origin concerns a source’s creator, date, place and circumstances; purpose concerns what it was intended to do and for whom. These features matter through the historical question. A campaign leaflet may reveal the public case a candidate chose to make, while providing weaker evidence about how residents privately felt. Read the content alongside the provenance so that an evaluation explains a specific connection rather than treating a source type as inherently trustworthy or useless.

Value and limitation can coexist. A source close to an event may record immediate concerns but have a restricted viewpoint. A later account may use additional evidence while also reflecting hindsight. Where purpose is inferred, identify the cue and qualify the inference. Corroboration requires more than counting similar accounts: several publications may repeat the same report. The fictional teaching extracts below practise these distinctions; they are not archival documents or evidence of real events.
keyIdeas: Value depends on the question.
Provenance supports reasoning, not a fixed score.
Agreement is stronger when sources are independent.

definitions.meaning: The creator, time, place and circumstances of a source’s production.
What the creator sought to achieve through the source, when supported by evidence.
A reason a source cannot securely answer some part of the chosen question.

method: State the historical question.
Identify relevant content and supplied provenance.
Explain one specific value and one specific limitation.
Identify independent evidence that could check the claim.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a ferry company’s launch leaflet promises “A reliable crossing for every worker”. Evaluate it for a question about the company’s public priorities.
steps: The company is the creator and the launch leaflet addresses potential users.
The promise foregrounds reliability and workers as an intended market, directly supporting a claim about public priorities.
A promotional promise does not show actual punctuality or equal access; service logs and user accounts would address those questions.
workedExample.conclusion: The leaflet is useful evidence of how the company presented its service. Its claim about performance requires separate evidence.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing “biased, therefore useless”.
misconceptions.correction: Explain what the perspective reveals and which question it limits.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling two copied reports independent corroboration.
misconceptions.correction: Check whether they rely on a common source.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching source: a town clerk writes meeting minutes the day after a council vote. Identify two supplied features of its origin.
hints: Use the creator and timing.
solution: The creator is the town clerk.
The minutes were written the day after the vote.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a worker’s letter to a friend describes one noisy factory shift. Evaluate its use for investigating that worker’s experience and all factories in the region.
hints: Compare the narrow and broad questions.
solution: The letter can reveal the worker’s reported experience of that shift.
Its recipient and circumstances may shape what the worker selects or leaves out.
One worker and shift cannot establish conditions across every regional factory.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: three newspapers print an identical station-opening report supplied by the railway company. Does agreement independently verify the claimed punctual service?
hints: Track the shared origin.
solution: The accounts repeat one company report, so they are not three independent observations.
They show circulation of the company’s claim.
Independent running records or passenger evidence would be needed to check punctuality.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: a shipping ledger lists arrivals every day for one month. Give a value and a limitation for an inquiry into annual port activity.
hints: Systematic entries provide detail.
One month does not cover seasonal variation.
solution: The ledger supports detailed arrival patterns during the recorded month.
It cannot alone establish the annual pattern because other months and seasonal changes are missing.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: a memoir written forty years later describes the author’s first school day. Identify one possible value and one limitation without dismissing it.
hints: Personal recollection can reveal experience and later meaning.
Time can affect recall.
solution: It may reveal the author’s remembered experience and the meaning attached to schooling.
The delay can affect exact detail, so contemporary records can help check chronology without removing the memoir’s interpretive value.

checklist: I explain both value and limit.

notes.title: An inspection’s scope limits its inference
paragraphs: Origin and purpose matter because they shape access to information, selection and presentation. An official inspection report may have systematic observations unavailable to a casual visitor, yet its inspection schedule and reporting remit can leave experiences unrecorded. Value and limitation should connect these features to a specific question. Avoid stock labels such as primary therefore reliable or official therefore false. A source can be near an event but narrowly informed, while a later study may combine many records. Evaluate what the author could know, what the format encourages and which claims remain beyond the evidence supplied.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a factory inspector visits one workshop on a scheduled morning and records machine guards. Assess value and limitation for everyday safety.
steps: The inspector directly records a safety feature during the visit, providing specific evidence about guards that morning.
A scheduled visit may not represent all shifts or normal practice, and guards alone do not measure every hazard.
workedExamples.conclusion: The report supports a bounded observation rather than a complete safety history.

flashcards.back: Creator, date, place and circumstances of production, when supplied.
The intended function or effect of the source.
As usefulness for a specified historical question.
Institutional status alone does not establish completeness or accuracy.

diagrams.title: An inspection’s scope limits its inference
diagrams.description: Direct observation has value within the time and features inspected.

nodes.label: Historical scope
nodes.detail: Evidence for that visit, not every shift or hazard

edges.label: provides direct access to one setting

lessons.summary: Explain consequences through mechanisms, time frames and uneven effects while separating intended aims from observed outcomes.
objectives: Distinguish an aim from an outcome.
Trace a supported chain of consequences.
Evaluate differences across groups and time periods.
explanation: A consequence is an outcome linked to an event, decision or process. A sequence alone does not establish the link: explain the mechanism and consider other influences. Distinguish what decision-makers intended from what evidence shows happened. An outcome can affect groups differently or become visible only later, so state the people, place and period covered by the judgement. A beneficial result for one group need not be beneficial for everyone.

Organise an account around supported relationships rather than a list of everything that happened afterwards. Direct consequences may lead to further effects, but each link needs evidence. An unintended consequence is one not part of the stated aim; it is not necessarily unpredictable or harmful. Where the records do not establish intentions, leave them uncertain. Use a conclusion that acknowledges missing observations and avoids turning a plausible explanation into a claim of inevitability.
keyIdeas: Later events are not automatically consequences.
Aims and outcomes need different evidence.
Effects differ across groups and times.

definitions.meaning: An outcome connected to an event or process by a supported causal relationship.
A result an actor aimed to produce.
A further outcome operating through an intervening effect.

method: Define the event and period examined.
Separate stated aims from recorded outcomes.
Trace mechanisms and alternative influences.
Compare effects across groups and state limits.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a council opens an evening market to extend trading hours. Shop records describe later closing; residents’ letters complain of nighttime noise. What consequences are supported?
steps: Later closing is consistent with the stated aim of extending trading hours.
The letters support complaints by their writers about noise, a different type of effect.
The evidence does not establish whether total trade increased or whether all residents objected.
workedExample.conclusion: The records support changed hours and reported disturbance, with different implications for traders and letter writers. Wider economic and community effects remain unmeasured.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a policy announcement as proof of success.
misconceptions.correction: Look for outcome evidence distinct from the announcement.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling every unintended effect harmful.
misconceptions.correction: Judge its nature separately from whether it was intended.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a notice says a bridge aims to shorten journeys; a later diary says one journey took less time. Distinguish aim and reported outcome.
hints: Which source announces and which reports?
solution: The notice states the intended shorter journeys.
The diary reports one traveller’s shorter journey, which supports a limited outcome claim.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a closed road redirects carts past a bakery; its records then show more passing customers. Explain a possible mechanism and a limitation.
hints: Trace access before inferring profit.
solution: The diversion brings cart traffic past the bakery and may increase potential customers.
Recorded passing customers support that intermediate effect.
They do not alone establish sales or profit, and other changes could also affect demand.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: after a new town hall opens, school attendance rises. No connecting evidence is supplied. Evaluate the claim that the hall caused the rise.
hints: Chronology does not supply the mechanism.
solution: The sequence is compatible with many explanations.
No evidence links the hall to attendance through a particular action or process.
Check school rules, transport, records and other contemporaneous changes before attributing the rise to the hall.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: a rule extends shop opening hours to improve access. Records show longer opening and higher lighting costs. Identify the intended and an additional consequence.
hints: Use the stated aim.
Separate service access from operating cost.
solution: Longer opening is consistent with the intended increase in access opportunities.
Higher lighting costs are an additional consequence, though actual customer access still needs usage evidence.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: a new road cuts travel time for central residents but not for residents beyond an unconnected river. Assess the claim “everyone benefited equally”.
hints: Compare the two groups.
Avoid averaging away unequal access.
solution: Central residents have a recorded travel-time benefit.
The unconnected group does not share that benefit, so the evidence contradicts an equal-benefit claim.

notes.title: Removing a toll can redistribute journeys
paragraphs: Consequences differ by group, place and timescale. A policy can achieve its stated aim while creating additional effects that were not intended. Distinguish an immediate administrative change from a later social outcome, and trace the mechanism connecting them. A new service may benefit those able to reach it while leaving distant communities underserved. The absence of an intended benefit does not automatically prove the policy had no effects. Historical evaluation should ask who experienced each consequence and use evidence appropriate to that group, rather than extending one person’s account to the entire population.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional case: a toll is removed from a bridge. Cart records show more crossings, while a ferry operator’s accounts show falling fares collected. Analyse two consequences.
steps: Removing the toll may encourage bridge use, consistent with the crossing increase.
Some travellers may switch from ferry to bridge, contributing to reduced ferry receipts.
workedExamples.conclusion: These are distinct possible consequences; route-choice evidence would strengthen the link to the ferry loss.

flashcards.back: An effect outside the intervention’s stated aims.

flashcards.front: Can one change benefit and harm different groups?
flashcards.back: Yes; consequences can be uneven.

flashcards.front: Why distinguish immediate and long-term effects?
flashcards.back: Different mechanisms and evidence may apply.
A supported causal mechanism.

diagrams.title: Removing a toll can redistribute journeys
diagrams.description: The same change can affect travellers and competing transport providers.

nodes.label: Ferry receipts fall
nodes.detail: Some journeys may move away from the ferry

edges.label: can reduce demand for the alternative

lessons.summary: Identify what persists across a defined period while testing whether apparent stability conceals changes in experience or evidence.
objectives: Compare like evidence at different points in time.
Distinguish stable institutions from stable lived experience.
Explain limits caused by gaps or changing records.
explanation: Continuity means persistence in a specified feature across time, rather than an absence of history. Define the feature and compare evidence from more than one point. A town may keep the same council structure while its membership or powers change. Be precise about what remains: the name, rule, practice or distribution of authority. A conclusion about one dimension should not become a claim that every aspect of life stayed the same.

The evidence itself can create misleading appearances. Repeated wording in an official register may reflect a fixed recording format, not identical experience. A gap in surviving records cannot establish uninterrupted stability, and two matching endpoints do not exclude changes between them. Examine intermediate evidence when available and compare what different groups experienced. Explain persistence alongside change, using time boundaries that the sources actually support.
keyIdeas: Continuity is a claim about a defined feature.
Stable labels can conceal changed practice.
Missing records do not prove no change.

definitions.meaning: Persistence of a specified feature over a defined period.
Comparison of observations at the beginning and end of a period.
Missing or unavailable material that limits what can be established.

method: Specify the feature and period.
Compare equivalent evidence at separate dates.
Check intermediate records and changing definitions.
State the extent and limits of persistence.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching case: registers from Year A and Year C use the same market-stall categories. No Year B register survives. Evaluate a claim that market life was completely unchanged.
steps: The endpoints show continuity in the recorded category labels.
The missing middle record leaves intervening changes unknown.
Even matching labels cannot establish unchanged goods, prices or traders’ experiences.
workedExample.conclusion: The strongest supported conclusion concerns the recording categories at the two endpoints. Complete continuity of market life goes beyond the evidence.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying nothing happened because an institution survived.
misconceptions.correction: Ask how its operation and people may have changed.

misconceptions.mistake: Using absent evidence as proof of stability.
misconceptions.correction: Treat gaps as limits unless evidence of expected recording supports a narrower inference.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: before and after a workshop expansion, the rules still require a morning safety check. Identify the specific continuity.
hints: Name the requirement, not all working conditions.
solution: The written requirement for a morning safety check persists.
The rules alone do not establish whether workers consistently performed it.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a school keeps the title “head teacher” while transferring budget decisions from the head teacher to a committee. Explain continuity and change.
hints: Compare the title with authority.
solution: The title continues.
Budget authority changes from the individual role to the committee.
Continuity in naming therefore coexists with change in governance.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a historian has identical rent amounts in two surviving ledgers ten years apart. Evaluate “rents never changed during the decade”.
hints: Do endpoints establish every intervening year?
solution: The ledgers show the same recorded amount at the two observed dates, assuming comparable properties and definitions.
They do not establish every intervening rent.
Seek intermediate records and comparable tenancy details before claiming uninterrupted stability.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: a town changes the market’s location but retains the same weekly trading day. State one continuity and one change.
hints: Separate time from place.
Use only supplied details.
solution: Continuity: the weekly trading day remains the same.
Change: the market location moves.

practice.prompt: Fictional records list the same apprenticeship fee in 1880 and 1900, with no intervening data. Is “the fee never changed for twenty years” justified?
hints: Endpoints do not show every intervening year.
State the narrower supported claim.
solution: The records show the same fee at the two surviving dates.
They do not exclude intervening rises or falls, so uninterrupted continuity is unproven.

checklist: I check gaps and intermediate years.
I allow continuity and change together.

notes.title: One institution can preserve and change different features
paragraphs: Continuity means persistence in a specified feature across a defined interval. It does not require every aspect of society to remain unchanged. An institution may keep its name and annual ceremony while changing who controls its decisions. Conversely, a new title may conceal familiar practices. Compare like evidence across time, including definitions and the groups represented. Two matching endpoint records establish similarity at those dates, but not necessarily uninterrupted stability between them. Gaps in the surviving record should therefore narrow the claim rather than be filled with an assumption that nothing happened.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional case: a guild keeps an annual procession, but its admission rules now include apprentices who were formerly excluded. Identify continuity and change.
steps: The annual procession persists, showing continuity in that public ritual.
Admission rules change, broadening formal participation.
workedExamples.conclusion: The case combines continuity in ceremony with change in membership rules.

flashcards.back: Yes, in different features of the same institution.

flashcards.front: What must a continuity claim specify?
flashcards.back: The feature and interval being compared.

flashcards.front: Do equal endpoint values prove an unchanged path?
flashcards.back: No; intermediate changes may be unrecorded.
A stable label may hide a changed meaning.

diagrams.title: One institution can preserve and change different features
diagrams.description: Ceremony and membership are separate dimensions.

lessons.summary: Explain the extent, pace and unevenness of change using defined comparisons and supported turning points.
objectives: Compare a feature across a stated period.
Distinguish extent from pace.
Evaluate turning points using evidence before and after them.
explanation: A claim of change compares a specified feature across time. Extent concerns how much altered; pace concerns how quickly. Define the period and group so that a large shift for one population is not assumed to apply to everyone. Changes in law, infrastructure or membership can occur at different rates from changes in everyday practice. Use comparable evidence and explain what each source actually measures.

A turning point is an event or interval argued to redirect a longer pattern. Its importance needs evidence from before and after, rather than only a memorable date. A new policy may announce a change whose implementation is delayed or uneven. Describing change as progress or decline introduces a judgement that depends on criteria and perspective. State the relevant standard, consider those who experienced different effects and avoid treating later outcomes as inevitable.
keyIdeas: Extent and pace answer different questions.
An announcement and implementation are distinct.
Turning points require a surrounding pattern.

definitions.meaning: The degree or reach of change in a specified feature.
The speed at which change occurs.
An event or interval supported as redirecting a broader pattern.

method: Define the feature, population and period.
Compare suitable before-and-after evidence.
Examine pace, unevenness and continuities.
Justify any turning-point or progress judgement.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a town implements a change from paid to free library entry in Year B. Entry registers show more visits in Year C, but the distant district still has no transport link. Evaluate the change.
steps: The rule changes access charges at the library.
More recorded visits in Year C are consistent with increased use, but do not by themselves establish the policy as the only cause.
The transport gap shows that removing a fee does not remove every barrier.
workedExample.conclusion: Access changed in one important respect, with evidence of later increased use. The evidence does not establish equally improved access for every district.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming a legal change instantly changes all behaviour.
misconceptions.correction: Examine implementation and lived experience.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling all change progress.
misconceptions.correction: Specify a criterion and whose experience is judged.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: one village replaces its footbridge in a week; another replaces several bridges over years. Explain why pace and extent should be distinguished.
hints: Speed and number of changed sites are different measures.
solution: The first replacement occurs quickly at one site.
The second process takes longer but covers several sites.
Neither description alone establishes which project better met local needs.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: new voting rules admit an additional group, but its turnout is initially low. Analyse what changed and what remains uncertain.
hints: Compare eligibility with participation.
solution: Formal eligibility expands.
Low initial turnout limits a claim of immediate broad participation.
Further evidence is needed about registration, access, choice and later turnout; low participation does not erase the eligibility change.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a new port opens, but trade had already grown for several years. Evaluate the claim that opening day alone was the turning point.
hints: Examine the earlier trend and later direction.
solution: The prior growth challenges a claim that the opening initiated all expansion.
Compare growth, routes or trading relationships before and after opening to identify any redirection.
The port may accelerate an existing process; a turning-point judgement needs a stated dimension and supporting pattern.

practice.prompt: Fictional case: one town electrifies all streets in ten years; another electrifies one street in one month. Compare pace and extent.
hints: Use time for pace and coverage for extent.
Avoid one unqualified ranking.
solution: The second town’s stated project is faster in calendar time but covers only one street.
The first has broader stated coverage over a longer interval, so faster does not mean more extensive.

practice.prompt: Fictional data show literacy rising steadily before and after a school law at the same rate. Does the date alone establish a turning point in the trend?
hints: Look for a change in the trend.
A law can matter without changing this measured slope.
solution: The supplied series shows no change in the measured rate at that date.
The law may have other significance, but calling it a turning point in literacy growth needs additional evidence.

notes.title: Formal change can precede practical access
paragraphs: Analysing change requires a baseline, a later comparison and a stated dimension. Pace describes how quickly something changes; extent describes how widely or deeply it changes. A rapidly passed law may take years to alter everyday practice, and implementation can differ across places. A turning point should mark a supported alteration in direction, pace or structure rather than simply being a memorable date. Compare evidence before and after the proposed point while considering trends already underway. Distinguish formal eligibility, practical access and actual participation, since progress on one does not guarantee the others.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional case: an education rule admits girls immediately, but classrooms are added gradually over five years. Analyse pace of formal and practical change.
steps: Formal eligibility changes at the rule’s introduction.
Practical capacity expands gradually as classrooms are added, so access may lag behind eligibility.
workedExamples.conclusion: The case shows rapid legal change alongside slower implementation.

flashcards.back: The speed of change.
The scope or depth of change.
No; practical barriers may remain.

flashcards.front: What supports calling an event a turning point?
flashcards.back: Evidence of a changed direction, pace or structure.

diagrams.title: Formal change can precede practical access
diagrams.description: A rule and its implementation operate on different timescales.

nodes.label: Practical access
nodes.detail: Opportunities increase as facilities become available

edges.label: translates formal rights into usable places

lessons.summary: Reconstruct supported viewpoints in context while distinguishing understanding, agreement and invented inner thoughts.
objectives: Connect a viewpoint to supplied circumstances.
Compare perspectives without treating groups as uniform.
Recognise limits of surviving accounts.
explanation: Historical perspective involves understanding how people’s circumstances, available knowledge and values shaped their views. It requires evidence, not an imagined diary written from a modern standpoint. Distinguish what an actor could know then from what later outcomes make visible now. Explaining a belief in context does not require agreeing with it, and disagreement does not remove the need to understand its sources.

People in the same place or social group can hold conflicting views. Use actual statements or documented actions to support a perspective, and explain where inference begins. Public speech, private correspondence and retrospective memory may reveal different aspects of a viewpoint. Surviving records are uneven: an absent account is not evidence that a person lacked a view. Identify whose perspectives are represented and what further material could broaden the inquiry without inventing missing testimony.
keyIdeas: Context helps explain a view without endorsing it.
Groups contain differences.
Missing voices must not be filled with invented testimony.

definitions.meaning: A viewpoint shaped by position, experience, values and available knowledge.
Knowledge of later outcomes applied when looking back.
Interpreting the past as if people shared present-day knowledge or assumptions without examining context.

method: Identify the speaker and supplied circumstances.
Separate their known information from later knowledge.
Compare supported priorities or interpretations.
State whose viewpoint is missing and avoid invention.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a trader’s petition supports a new road because it shortens deliveries; a farmer’s letter opposes the route because it divides a field. Compare perspectives.
steps: The trader foregrounds delivery access, while the farmer foregrounds the use of a particular field.
Their interests help explain different responses to the same route.
Neither source represents every trader or farmer, and the farmer need not oppose roads in general.
workedExample.conclusion: The accounts reveal different local stakes. Understanding those stakes does not establish which proposal is best or justify treating either group as unanimous.

misconceptions.mistake: Inventing thoughts to make an account feel empathetic.
misconceptions.correction: Reconstruct only what evidence can support and mark uncertainty.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a whole group as one voice.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the particular people and evidence represented.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: an apprentice writes that evening classes conflict with a work shift. Explain the supported concern.
hints: Keep the inference tied to the stated conflict.
solution: The apprentice is concerned about the overlap between class and work time.
The statement does not prove opposition to education itself.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a council notice calls a square renovation “renewal”; a stallholder’s letter says it removes a trading place. Compare the framing.
hints: Connect labels with stated interests.
solution: “Renewal” frames the work as improvement in the council’s public notice.
The letter foregrounds loss of trading space for that stallholder.
The contrast supports differing priorities; it does not establish the views of all residents or the final balance of effects.

practice.prompt: A response claims people should have predicted a later flood, but the fictional source packet supplies no warning or contemporary forecast. Evaluate the reasoning.
hints: Separate later outcome from information then available.
solution: Knowledge that a flood later occurred does not establish that those people could predict it.
Investigate warnings, local knowledge and available information at the time.
Judging decisions requires that context rather than assuming later knowledge was already available.

practice.prompt: Fictional statements: a passenger values a faster express train; a village shopkeeper objects that it no longer stops locally. Compare the stated priorities.
hints: Identify the benefit each person emphasises.
Neither statement proves the other is false.
solution: The passenger prioritises journey speed; the shopkeeper prioritises local stopping access.
A faster service can reduce local access, so the disagreement concerns trade-offs as well as experience.

practice.prompt: A fictional 1890 planner lacks later flood records. A student argues the planner deliberately ignored a flood that occurred in 1920. Evaluate the inference.
hints: Later occurrence is not earlier knowledge.
Intent requires evidence of contemporary awareness.
solution: The 1920 event cannot by itself show what the planner knew in 1890.
Contemporary warnings or records would be needed to support deliberate disregard; the supplied claim uses hindsight.

checklist: I do not invent missing voices.

notes.title: One development can be experienced differently
paragraphs: A historical perspective reflects a person’s position, experiences and available information, but it should not be reduced to a stereotype about their group. Different accounts may focus on different consequences rather than directly contradict each other. A merchant may describe easier deliveries while a nearby resident describes noise; both can be accurate about their own concerns. Reconstruct the choices and information available at the time before evaluating decisions. Later knowledge can explain outcomes, but attributing that knowledge to earlier actors without evidence creates hindsight error. Supported comparison uses specific details rather than invented motives.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional teaching statements about a dock expansion: a carrier welcomes shorter unloading waits; a resident reports louder nights. Compare perspectives.
steps: The carrier focuses on transport efficiency, while the resident focuses on living conditions.
Shorter waits and more noise can coexist, so the statements are not necessarily factually inconsistent.
workedExamples.conclusion: The supplied concerns support a difference in priorities, not a claim about every carrier or resident.

flashcards.front: Can different perspectives both be accurate?
flashcards.back: Yes, if they describe different experiences or effects.
Attributing later knowledge to people who did not have it.
Individuals within a group may differ.
By specific supplied words, actions or circumstances.

diagrams.title: One development can be experienced differently
diagrams.description: Efficiency and living conditions are distinct criteria.

edges.label: coexists with a different local cost

lessons.summary: Justify historical significance through explicit criteria, supported effects and the inquiry being pursued.
objectives: Define a criterion for significance.
Use evidence to compare importance.
Distinguish significance, fame and moral approval.
explanation: Historical significance is an argued judgement about why something matters to an inquiry. Criteria might include the reach, duration or depth of consequences, or what a particular case reveals about a wider process. State the criterion and connect it to evidence. Fame, textbook space or personal interest can prompt a question, but none alone demonstrates significance. A local event may matter greatly for a focused inquiry even if it affected few people.

Significance can be assessed differently for different questions and communities. Compare candidates using a consistent criterion, and explain trade-offs when one had wider reach while another produced deeper local effects. Historical significance does not mean moral approval: harmful actions can have major consequences. A later commemoration is evidence of how people remembered an event, but does not by itself establish the original event’s impact or every person’s view of it.
keyIdeas: Criteria make significance arguable.
Importance depends partly on the inquiry.
Significance is separate from approval or fame.

definitions.meaning: Argued importance in relation to a historical question and stated criteria.
The breadth of people, places or activities affected.
An act or practice of remembering a person or event publicly.

method: Specify the inquiry and criterion.
Select evidence of effects or what the case reveals.
Compare alternatives using the same standard.
Qualify the judgement and separate memory from original impact.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a one-day parade drew a large crowd; a small evening school operated for decades. Compare their significance for an inquiry into sustained access to education.
steps: The inquiry makes duration and educational access relevant criteria.
The school’s continued operation is more directly relevant to that criterion than the parade’s crowd size.
Operation alone does not establish who attended or what they learned, so enrolment and experience records would strengthen the judgement.
workedExample.conclusion: The school is the stronger candidate for this inquiry, with important evidential limits. Another inquiry into public celebrations could reasonably prioritise the parade.

misconceptions.mistake: Equating significance with being admirable.
misconceptions.correction: Judge impact or explanatory value separately from moral approval.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling something important only because it is famous.
misconceptions.correction: Support a relevant criterion with evidence.

practice.prompt: For a fictional inquiry into a water service’s long-term effects, propose a relevant significance criterion and matching evidence.
hints: Link the criterion to a record.
solution: Duration of reliable access is a relevant criterion.
Maintenance and service records across the period could help assess it, alongside users’ accounts.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: one reform changes rules across a region; another changes daily routines in one town. Explain why a significance ranking needs more than place count.
hints: Consider depth as well as breadth.
solution: Regional scope indicates wider formal reach.
A local reform may have deeper effects on everyday experience.
Choose and justify a criterion for the inquiry, then obtain evidence about implementation and duration before ranking overall importance.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a monument was built long after an event. Evaluate “the monument proves everyone at the time thought the event important”.
hints: Whose time and whose decision does it directly record?
solution: The monument directly records a later commemorative decision.
It does not establish unanimous opinion when the original event happened.
Contemporary accounts and the monument’s commissioning records answer different questions about original response and later memory.

practice.prompt: For a fictional inquiry into access to public reading, propose one significance criterion for a travelling library and matching evidence.
hints: Focus on access rather than publicity.
Choose a measurable or documentable effect.
solution: A relevant criterion is whether previously underserved communities gained sustained access.
Route records, borrowing registers and users’ accounts over time could show reach and continued use.

practice.prompt: A fictional event receives little newspaper coverage but changes inheritance rights for a small excluded group. Does limited coverage prove insignificance?
hints: Publicity and depth of effect differ.
Consider the affected group and the inquiry.
solution: Limited coverage measures attention, not the depth of the legal change.
The event may be highly significant for that group’s rights; evaluate scope, duration and consequences rather than coverage alone.

notes.title: Criteria change a significance judgement
paragraphs: Historical significance is an argued judgement based on criteria, not simply a synonym for famous. An event may matter because of its scale, duration, depth of effects or what it reveals about a wider process. The relevant criteria depend on the inquiry. A small local initiative may be important for studying exclusion even if it affected fewer people than a national celebration. Later remembrance provides evidence about how subsequent societies interpreted the past, not automatic proof of contemporary importance. Explain why a chosen criterion matters and apply it consistently to the compared cases.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional case: a short exhibition attracts 20,000 visitors; a small archive preserves workers’ letters for decades. Compare significance for researching everyday working life.
steps: The exhibition has greater immediate attendance, but attendance is not the inquiry’s only criterion.
The archive’s preserved testimony may provide deeper and longer-lasting evidence of everyday work.
workedExamples.conclusion: For this inquiry, evidential depth and survival can outweigh visitor numbers.

flashcards.front: Is fame the same as historical significance?
flashcards.back: No; significance requires relevant criteria.
How long effects or influence persist.

flashcards.front: What does a later memorial directly show?
flashcards.back: Later remembrance and interpretation.

flashcards.front: Why state the inquiry when ranking significance?
flashcards.back: Different questions make different effects important.

diagrams.title: Criteria change a significance judgement
diagrams.description: A large audience and durable evidence answer different questions.

edges.label: evidential depth can support a different judgement

lessons.summary: Build a historical argument whose claims, evidence and qualifications answer a defined question.
objectives: Develop a thesis with clear scope.
Organise paragraphs around reasoning rather than chronology alone.
Use counterevidence to refine a conclusion.
explanation: A historical essay answers a question through an argument supported by evidence. Begin by identifying the task, period and terms that require definition, such as success or importance. A thesis should offer a defensible answer and indicate its limits. A chronological account may establish sequence, but it becomes an argument only when it explains how events relate to the question and why the evidence supports the judgement.

Give each paragraph a claim, relevant evidence and reasoning that connects them. Evaluate source limitations where they affect the inference instead of inserting a generic reliability paragraph unrelated to the argument. Counterevidence can qualify a claim without destroying it. A conclusion should weigh the established reasoning rather than add unexamined material. When a task restricts you to a supplied packet, do not fill gaps with invented dates, quotations or outcomes.
keyIdeas: A thesis answers a scoped question.
Evidence needs an explained connection.
Counterevidence can refine rather than erase a claim.

definitions.meaning: The essay’s central, supported answer to its question.
A reasoned challenge to part of the argument.
A stated limit on the scope or certainty of a claim.

method: Define the question, period and judgement criteria.
Draft a qualified thesis from available evidence.
Plan claims with evidence and reasoning.
Weigh counterevidence and conclude within the scope.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching packet: after a ferry opens, dock records show regular crossings, while island letters report unaffordable fares. Plan an answer to “How far did access improve?”
steps: Define access to include service availability and affordability.
Argue that availability improved for potential travellers, while affordability remained a barrier for the letter writers.
Use one paragraph on crossings and another on fares, then explain why the evidence does not support equal benefit for everyone.
workedExample.conclusion: A qualified thesis is that the ferry improved the opportunity to cross while leaving a documented cost barrier. The packet cannot establish every household’s experience.

misconceptions.mistake: Retelling events without answering the question.
misconceptions.correction: Make each paragraph advance a claim relevant to the judgement.

misconceptions.mistake: Adding invented details to make an argument sound complete.
misconceptions.correction: State the evidential gap and keep the answer appropriately narrow.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching packet: a new school building has more classrooms but no additional teachers yet. Write a qualified thesis about expanded teaching capacity.
hints: Distinguish space from staffing.
solution: Physical capacity expanded, but the packet does not establish whether staffing and timetabling allow increased teaching provision.
The claim recognises the additional rooms without assuming an immediate increase in teaching provision.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching case: a paragraph claims a library served the whole town, but its cited register covers only members who could pay a fee. Explain a revision.
hints: Does membership evidence cover everyone?
solution: Narrow the claim to the recorded paying membership.
Explain how the fee and register scope limit conclusions about access by non-members.
Identify additional evidence needed about excluded groups instead of asserting universal service.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching packet: a leader’s speech promises jobs; no employment record is supplied. Evaluate an essay conclusion claiming the promise was fulfilled.
hints: A statement of intent is not an outcome record.
solution: The speech supports a claim about the leader’s public promise.
It does not establish that jobs were created.
Revise the conclusion to distinguish the promise from an unverified result and identify outcome records needed.

practice.prompt: Fictional packet: a town installs more pumps, but records show frequent breakdowns. Write a one-sentence judgement about water access.
hints: Separate installed capacity from reliable service.
Include both pieces of evidence.
solution: Possible answer: The pumps expanded potential access, but frequent breakdowns limited the reliability of the improvement.
This uses the additional infrastructure as support while allowing the maintenance evidence to qualify actual service.

practice.prompt: A fictional essay says “the reform helped all workers” but cites only accounts from skilled workers. Revise the claim and identify needed evidence.
hints: Match the population in the claim to the sources.
Other worker groups need representation.
solution: Revise to say the supplied skilled-worker accounts describe benefits for those workers.
Seek evidence from other occupational groups before extending the judgement to all workers.

checklist: I keep the conclusion within scope.

notes.title: Evidence shapes the scope of the thesis
paragraphs: A historical argument should answer the question through a claim that the evidence can sustain. Each paragraph needs a clear analytical role rather than merely another event in chronological order. Use evidence to support a mechanism, comparison or qualification, and explain that connection. Counter-evidence should change the scope or strength of the judgement where appropriate. A conclusion can be decisive while remaining bounded: a reform may improve formal access substantially but leave practical barriers. Avoid treating a source’s promise as a measured outcome or extending evidence from one group to everyone without justification.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional packet: a public reading room removes entry fees; visits rise, but opening hours still exclude night-shift workers. Develop a thesis about access.
steps: Fee removal and increased visits support improved access for some users.
The opening-hours barrier limits the claim for night-shift workers.
workedExamples.conclusion: Thesis: access improved through lower cost and greater use, but remained uneven because time barriers persisted.

flashcards.back: Answer the question with a supportable judgement.
Explaining how it supports or limits the claim.
The scope, strength or conditions of the conclusion.

flashcards.front: Can a qualified thesis still be clear?
flashcards.back: Yes; it can state both the supported improvement and its limit.

diagrams.title: Evidence shapes the scope of the thesis
diagrams.description: A benefit and a barrier must both influence the final judgement.

nodes.label: Fee removed; visits rise
nodes.detail: Evidence of improved affordability and use

edges.label: limit the conclusion to supported groups

lessons.summary: Answer source tasks by matching the command to a clear inference, comparison or evaluation grounded in the supplied material.
objectives: Distinguish inference, comparison and evaluation tasks.
Integrate content and provenance where relevant.
Synthesize a qualified answer across a source packet.
explanation: A source-based question may ask you to infer, compare, evaluate or use a packet to answer a broader question. Identify the command before writing. An inference moves from a detail to a supported conclusion; comparison relates sources on the same point; evaluation explains what evidence can establish for a specified purpose. None is completed by paraphrasing every source without explaining its relevance to the task.

Read provenance and content together, keeping each source’s date, viewpoint and scope visible. Two sources can agree about one detail while differing about its meaning, and agreement may depend on a shared origin. In a packet-based judgement, use both supporting and complicating material, stating what remains unknown. Refer to supplied labels accurately and never attribute a quotation to a historical person when it is a fictional teaching extract. Alternative answers can be defensible when they account for the same evidence.
keyIdeas: The command determines the reasoning needed.
Agreement and difference can coexist.
A packet supports a bounded judgement, not every possible claim.

definitions.meaning: A conclusion drawn from specified evidence rather than merely copied from it.
An explanation of a meaningful relationship between sources.
A judgement that brings relevant evidence together while accounting for differences and limits.

method: Identify command, focus and source labels.
Select precise content and relevant provenance.
Explain the inference, relationship or limitation.
Form a qualified answer that accounts for competing evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional teaching packet: A, a council notice, announces a free well; B, a resident’s letter, says “The well is free, but the queue makes me late.” Compare their evidence about access.
steps: Both present use of the well as free of charge.
A foregrounds provision; B reports a time cost for one resident.
The sources are compatible about price but differ in their view of practical access.
workedExample.conclusion: The packet supports free-of-charge access while preserving evidence of another barrier. The letter cannot establish the length or effect of every queue.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing the same answer for infer, compare and evaluate.
misconceptions.correction: Match the reasoning to the actual command.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating different emphasis as proof one source is false.
misconceptions.correction: Check whether their claims contradict or describe different dimensions.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching source A is a petition requesting lamps on an unlit route used after evening work. Infer one concern, using a detail.
hints: Connect the request with the route’s use.
solution: The petitioners are concerned about travelling along the route after dark.
The request for lamps on a route used after evening work supports that inference; it does not establish a specific accident.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching packet: A, a station notice, says the waiting room closes at dusk. B, a traveller’s diary, describes waiting outside after dusk. Compare the accounts.
hints: Are these contradictory?
solution: Both are consistent with the indoor waiting area being unavailable after dusk.
A states a rule; B describes one traveller’s experience compatible with it.
The diary does not establish that every traveller waited outside or that the rule was enforced on every evening.

practice.prompt: Fictional teaching packet: A is a mayor’s claim that a new hall welcomes all clubs; B is a booking record showing only two clubs used it in its first week. Evaluate whether the packet proves exclusion of other clubs.
hints: Distinguish use, eligibility and a short observation window.
solution: The claim concerns intended or stated access, while the record shows actual bookings in one week.
Limited use does not by itself prove other clubs were barred; demand, awareness or scheduling could differ.
Eligibility rules, rejected requests and a longer booking record would help evaluate exclusion.

practice.prompt: Fictional packet: a theatre notice offers discounted student tickets; a student diary says tickets were discounted but sold out. State one agreement and one additional detail.
hints: Find the shared ticket-price fact.
Separate affordability from availability.
solution: Both sources support the existence of a student discount.
The diary adds a supply limit: discounted tickets were unavailable because they had sold out.

practice.prompt: Fictional packet: a council claims every street was cleaned daily; a dated diary reports one uncleaned street on a stated day. What can the packet establish if the diary is credible?
hints: Test the word every.
Do not infer a town-wide failure rate from one instance.
solution: The diary provides a counterexample to universal daily cleaning.
It does not establish how frequently streets were missed or the overall quality of the service.

notes.title: A service rule and an experience answer different questions
paragraphs: Source-based answers need to distinguish agreement, difference and the scope of each source. Two sources may agree on a rule while disagreeing about its effects, or cover different dates rather than genuinely conflict. Identify the precise claim being compared and quote or paraphrase only the relevant detail. When evaluating a packet, use sources together without assuming the packet is complete. An official announcement can establish an intended change, while a user account may illuminate implementation. A small number of accounts can challenge a universal claim but rarely establishes how common an experience was across an entire population.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional packet: A announces a new postal delivery every weekday; B is a resident’s diary reporting no delivery on two listed weekdays. Compare the evidence.
steps: A states the intended schedule; B reports exceptions experienced by one resident.
The diary challenges perfect implementation of the schedule but does not show that all deliveries failed.
workedExamples.conclusion: Use both to distinguish the service rule from local experience.

flashcards.front: What should a comparison identify first?
flashcards.back: The specific claim or feature shared by the sources.

flashcards.front: Can an exception challenge a universal claim?
flashcards.back: Yes, if the exception is credible and relevant.

flashcards.front: Does one exception reveal its frequency?
flashcards.back: No; broader coverage is needed.

flashcards.front: What differs between a schedule and a diary?
flashcards.back: An intended rule versus an account of experienced events.

diagrams.title: A service rule and an experience answer different questions
diagrams.description: A reported exception limits a claim of perfect implementation.

nodes.label: Combined interpretation
nodes.detail: Intended service existed, but reported delivery was imperfect
